articles.title: Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif to meet Donald Trump on September 23 during UNGA in New York: Report
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is set to meet US President Donald Trump in New York on September 23 during the United Nations General Assembly.
articles.body: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is set to meet US President Donald Trump in New York on September 23 during the United Nations General Assembly week, according to a media report cited by news agency PTI.Sharif is among the world leaders invited to a reception dinner being hosted by Trump and First Lady Melania Trump on September 23, The News reported, citing high-level sources.The event is scheduled at the Lotte New York Palace Hotel on Madison Avenue.The dinner could give Sharif an opportunity to hold discussions with Trump as well as other heads of state and government attending the UNGA.The proposed meeting comes months after the two leaders met at the inaugural Board of Peace meeting in Washington in February. They had previously held talks at the White House in September 2025 and met again during the Sharm el-Sheikh Peace Summit in Egypt in October last year.Sharif is expected to arrive in New York on September 22 and address the UN General Assembly on September 25. According to the report, he is likely to use his address to raise Pakistan's concerns over India's decision to keep the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance.India suspended the 1960 treaty in April 2025 following the Pahalgam terror attack that killed 26 civilians. New Delhi said the pact would remain in abeyance until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably ended its support for crossborder terrorism.The Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank, sets out the framework for sharing the waters of six rivers in the Indus river system between the two countries.Sharif is also expected to speak about Pakistan's new security partnership with Saudi Arabia and Turkey. The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, creating a collective defence framework under which an attack on one member would be considered an attack on all three.The 81st UN General Assembly's high-level General Debate will be held from September 22 to 26 and on September 28 at the UN headquarters in New York. Sharif is scheduled to speak fourth during the second half of the session on September 25.Shehbaz Sharif's proposed meeting with Trump comes against the backdrop of India's diplomatic engagement with major global powers, highlighted by the Brics Summit 2026 hosted by New Delhi.The summit brought together leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, underlining India's role in engaging with key powers across geopolitical blocs.Prime Minister Narendra Modi also announced the unanimous adoption of the New Delhi Declaration by Brics leaders.The summit also saw Brics leaders condemn the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir. In their joint statement, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and called for a policy of zero tolerance towards terrorism.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump calls on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel, saying attacks are causing a shortage
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian diesel, saying the attacks are causing a g...
articles.body:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage. He spoke after diesel prices in the U.S. hit a record on Friday , soaring past $6 a gallon on average.

Ukraine has for months been targeting Russia's oil and gas industry with long-range strikes, prompting fuel rationing across the country and causing Moscow to ban diesel exports in July, one factor disrupting the global supply of diesel. But the global crunch also came after the war on Iran curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Fuel prices are weighing on Americans as they prepare to vote in midterm elections in November.

Trump was asked by a reporter if he had spoken with Zelenskyy following his recent conversation with Russia's Vladimir Putin. He responded by calling on Zelenskyy to halt strikes against Russia.

"Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the Irish Open, which is being played at his Doonbeg golf club.

"We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel, because that's hurting, that's hurting the world," he said.

Kyiv says Russia's oil industry both funds and directly fuels Moscow's more than four-year-old invasion of its neighbor.

Russia has ramped up its air campaign against Ukraine in recent weeks, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce Ukraine's defenses. Moscow's attacks have targeted Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter in what officials say is meant to demoralize civilians.

Civilians were killed and injured overnight into Sunday as Russia and Ukraine exchanged large-scale drone strikes.

Two people were killed and 14 more injured near an oil and industrial hub in Russia's Tatarstan, according to local officials, while Ukrainian authorities reported on reported on Russian drones pummelling the Black Sea port of Odesa and starting a fire near a border crossing with Poland.

Ukraine targets more Russian oil facilities

The two Russian civilians died after a drone slammed into a tree near their parked car in the city of Nizhnekamsk, according to the office of regional head Rustam Minnikhanov. Nizhnekamsk houses a key cluster of oil refineries and other industrial plants. Mayor Radmir Belyaev said that a fire had broken out at an unspecified "enterprise."

Ukraine also claimed to have hit a major oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban, in Russia's Krasnodar region near Crimea. The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) agency said its drones struck a key oil processing unit and the refinery's tank farm overnight into Sunday.

Krasnodar authorities said the strike on "an enterprise" in Slavyansk-on-Kuban injured three people and damaged an oil pipeline.

Russian forces shot down 389 Ukrainian drones during the night, Russia's defense ministry said Sunday.

Russia targets Odesa and western Ukraine

In Ukraine, at least nine people were injured in a "massive" Russian nighttime attack on Odesa, according to Serhii Lysak from the city's military administration. Odesa is home to Ukraine's main port hub on the Black Sea and has faced sustained drone and missile strikes, with Kyiv accusing Moscow of trying to choke off its exports.

A Russian drone attack on Saturday struck a residential high-rise in Odesa , killing two people and injuring 26 others, Ukrainian officials said.

Russian overnight strikes also pounded western Ukraine, though there were no immediate reports of casualties. One drone set fire to a gas station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing with Poland, according to Ukraine's top diplomat and a spokesperson for the local customs force.

"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X.

Ukraine's border crossings with Poland are a conduit for much of the military and humanitarian aid sent by Western allies.

Valentyna Chernysh, a spokesperson for the Volyn Customs Office, told The Associated Press that the Yahodyn crossing was intact and no one was harmed.

Earlier this week, two people died when Russian drones hit the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova on Tuesday. The following day a "direct threat" to a Polish-Ukrainian crossing point was avoided due to the cooperation between Warsaw and Kyiv, according to Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Ukraine's air force said its air defenses shot down or suppressed 409 Russian drones of various types overnight, including a newer jet-powered version that is faster and more difficult to intercept. It said Russia had attacked Ukraine with 453 drones in total.

Kremlin says peace talks could restart in October

Also on Sunday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow is open to restarting peace talks in autumn featuring Russia, Ukraine and the U.S.

"We are not ruling out that possibility," Peskov told reporters. "October cannot be ruled out."

Last weekend, U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, followed by a meeting with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv. Despite the latest diplomatic push, the core demands of Moscow and Kyiv remain mutually exclusive, especially over territorial concessions.

articles.title: Indian-origin Fiji minister Agni Deo Singh dies in Brisbane during Australia visit at 60
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Agni Deo Singh, Fiji's Minister for Employment, passed away at 60 in Brisbane while attending the Fiji-Australia Vuvale Partnership, leaving a legacy of improved workers' rights and wages in Fiji.
articles.body: Indian-origin Fiji minister Agni Deo Singh died in Brisbane during an Australian visit on September 12, the country's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka announced the death on the official Fiji Government Facebook page.Singh served as Fiji's Minister for Employment, Productivity and Workplace Relations from 2023 to 2026.Singh had been in Australia as part of a delegation working under the Fiji-Australia Vuvale Partnership. The group included representatives from Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and Department of Employment and Workplace Relations and was visiting Fijian workers employed under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme.During the Brisbane visit, Singh met Fijian PALM workers at Australian Country Choice and held discussions with company and labour-hire representatives. He acknowledged the company for employing Fijian workers and heard feedback from them, according to Australia Today.He also visited JBS Australia, where he commended the company's focus on worker welfare and wellbeing. Singh welcomed its commitment to transparency around wages and deductions.Fiji's Minister for Fisheries and Forestry Alitia Bainivalu also paid tribute to Singh, highlighting his work on employment and workers' rights during his time in government.Under Singh's tenure, Fiji's national minimum wage rose from $4 to $4.50 an hour in 2024 and then to $5 an hour in 2025. The full 18% Fiji National Provident Fund contribution was also restored in 2024, strengthening workers' retirement savings.Bainivalu also credited Singh's ministry with helping resolve a decades-long dispute involving 368 Vatukoula mine workers. A $9.2 million settlement awarded $25,000 to each worker, ending a dispute that had remained unresolved for more than 30 years.She said Singh's tenure also saw the restoration of freedom of association, greater engagement between the government, employers and unions, and increased attention to workplace grievances, wages and employment conditions.“His legacy will not only be remembered in Parliament or in Government records. It will be remembered in the lives of ordinary working people,” Bainivalu said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Roaring deer leads alpine hiker to believe bear is after him
articles.summary: Alarmed by a loud roar, a hiker in the Allgäu Alps near Bad Hindelang in southern Germany called the police emergency number, believing he was about to be at...
articles.body:
Alarmed by a loud roar, a hiker in the Allgäu Alps near Bad Hindelang in southern Germany called the police emergency number, believing he was about to be attacked by a bear, officers said on Sunday.

The roaring could be clearly heard over the phone, police said. They identified the source of the roar as a male deer that was rutting, or making loud roaring sounds during the mating season.

After some reassurance from the officers, the hiker realized he was not in danger and managed to walk past the deer while keeping a safe distance.

The scenic region is a popular destination for hiking and for winter sports.

articles.title: Canada explores EU ‘associate membership’ as Carney seeks closer ties with Europe amid US trade war
articles.summary: Europe News: Canada is exploring whether it could become an “associate member” of the European Union as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks closer economic and strate.
articles.body: Canada is exploring whether it could become an “associate member” of the European Union as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks closer economic and strategic ties with the bloc, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.The EU, which has historically been reluctant to change its membership rules, is open to the idea of creating a new associate membership status for Canada, the newspaper reported, citing unnamed officials from both sides.The Canadian embassy in Brussels and the European Commission did not respond to separate requests for comment.Canada's worsening trade relationship with the United States has added urgency to its efforts to strengthen ties with other trading partners.Relations between Ottawa and Washington have deteriorated since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House in early 2025, with disagreements over trade and other issues leading to tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in cross-border trade.Canada and EU explore deeper economic linksCanada and the EU are discussing ways to allow goods, services and workers involved in strategic supply chains to move more freely between them, according to the Wall Street Journal report.The areas under discussion include energy, artificial intelligence, defence and critical minerals, effectively shifting the EU's economic border closer to Canada.The two sides are also discussing cooperation on underwater cables, data centres, cloud storage and new satellite networks and infrastructure to facilitate the shipment of Canadian energy to Europe, the report said.Carney has also held regular discussions with several EU leaders, particularly French President Emmanuel Macron, about the possibility of allowing Canadians to live and work in the EU without visas, according to two officials cited by the Wall Street Journal.Carney and Macron are scheduled to meet later this month. Macron's press office did not respond to a request for comment.Existing Canada-EU trade deal faces ratification hurdlesCloser institutional ties between Canada and the EU could face challenges, however, as even a more limited trade agreement between the two sides has encountered difficulties.The Canada-EU trade deal was struck more than a decade ago and provisionally entered into force nine years ago, but several EU countries have still not ratified it.The latest discussions therefore come as Canada seeks to deepen its relationship with Europe while its trade tensions with its largest trading partner, the United States, continue.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Plugging gap: Why 67,000 EV charging points aren't enough for India’s electric dreams
articles.summary: India News: When Siddharth Das, a Delhi-NCR based working professional and long-time motor enthusiast, traded in his petrol sedan for a brand-new electric SUV, he.
articles.body: When Siddharth Das, a Delhi-NCR based working professional and long-time motor enthusiast, traded in his petrol sedan for a brand-new electric SUV, he wasn’t just buying a new car. He was also trying to make his daily commute what he describes as "future-ready".But switching to an electric vehicle brought a different kind of calculation."My previous petrol car cost me 10 to 12 rupees a kilometre. With an EV, even if I use commercial chargers at 15 to 21 rupees per unit, my running cost is just 3 to 3.50 rupees a kilometre. If I could charge at domestic home rates of 8 rupees a unit, it would drop to 1 rupee per kilometre."However, Das faces a problem even before he leaves his residential building."I live in an apartment complex where parking is in the basement, and the society isn’t allowing home chargers due to safety protocol concerns," he explains.His experience shows one of the bigger challenges in India's shift to electric vehicles. The cars are improving quickly, but the charging system around them is still developing and can be difficult to access.67,000 plugs down, 13 lakhs to goAccording to a landmark study by Rubix Data Sciences released in September 2026, citing baseline projections from the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), India will need 13.2 lakh EV charging points by 2030 to support the growing number of electric vehicles.But how far is India from that target?Data from the Ministry of Heavy Industries shows that, as of August 2026, India had 67,657 public charging points across the country including 1,139 battery-swapping station interfaces. This is in comparison to only 5,000 public chargers in early 2022 and 29,151 in December 2025.But even after this growth, the current network is only about 5 percent of the 13.2 lakh charging points expected to be needed by 2030.In simple terms, India still needs to add more than 1.25 million to reach the projected requirement. This gap matters because the number of EVs on the road is also increasing, meaning charging infrastructure has to grow fast enough to keep up with vehicle sales.There is also a major geographical imbalance. The Rubix analysis says the top 10 states, led by Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh, account for 78 per cent of all public chargers in India.That means nearly four out of every five public chargers are concentrated in just 10 states. For EV users in other parts of the country, especially smaller towns and less-developed regions, finding a public charger can therefore be much harder.Power disconnect: Built for scooters, not long-haul tripsThe problem is not only the number of chargers. It is also how much power those chargers can provide.Out of the 66,518 non-swapping fixed chargers installed across the country as of August 2026, most are on the slower side:48,709 chargers, or about 73 percent, are rated below 30 kW.15,753 chargers are in the 30–60 kW range.1,513 chargers offer 61–120 kW fast charging.Only 534 chargers provide 121–240 kW, while just nine chargers offer more than 240 kW nationwide.These figures are important because a charger’s power rating affects how quickly an EV can be charged. A large network may therefore look impressive on paper, but if most chargers are low-power units, drivers travelling long distances may still have to spend considerable time charging.The current charging mix also reflects the kinds of electric vehicles being sold in India. Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA) figures cited in the study show that the switch to electric vehicles is currently strongest among three-wheelers, where EVs have a 60.77 per cent market penetration, and two-wheelers, at 8.88 per cent.Electric four-wheeler passenger cars have a much lower penetration of 5.70 percent.This helps explain why India has a large number of lower-powered chargers.Low-power AC chargers can work well for e-rickshaws, electric two-wheelers and vehicles used mainly for short city trips. But the same infrastructure is less suitable for electric cars travelling long distances or for heavy commercial vehicles that need to cover hundreds of kilometres.Divide in driver experience: Home charging vs range anxietyFor EV owners who have private parking and can install a home charger, everyday use can be relatively simple. Bishwajeet Kumar Seth, who bought his electric SUV in April 2026, relies entirely on home charging."I have a 7.2 kW charger installed at home," Seth says. "My car has a real-world range of around 550 km with the AC on. When I drove from Delhi to Mathura, I didn't even need to plug in on the road. At home, it costs me 7 to 8 rupees a unit. At a highway fast charger, they were charging 19 rupees per unit. I thought, why bear double the cost when I don't need to?"But the experience can be very different for people who do not own an EV or who rent one occasionally. For them, "range anxiety" remains a major concern.Mohammad Sarim, who rented an EV during a trip to Kerala, came away hesitant."I had the car for 12 hours to cover 150 km, but the display showed a total range of 200 km," he shares. "Being in the outskirts, I didn't spot a single charger. The anxiety of the battery running down made it feel less convenient than a petrol car"Saad Abbasi, a commuter in the NCR region, also says the lack of infrastructure affects buying decisions. "Unless you live in Central or South Delhi, NCR has limited infrastructure. It's fine for home-to-office daily commuting if you can charge at home, but the moment you travel away from major cities, it becomes an issue."Operator crisis: Empty stations in tier-2, tier-3 townsWhile EV buyers worry about finding a charger, charging operators face almost the opposite problem: their chargers often do not get enough customers.Data from the Rubix Data Sciences report shows that public chargers across India currently have a utilisation rate of only 1 to 5 per cent.This means that, for much of the time, many public chargers are sitting unused. That creates a difficult business case, particularly for operators in smaller cities and towns. They have to spend a large amount of money upfront, but may not have enough vehicles using the chargers to recover that investment quickly.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Amit Kumar Sahu, a fuel station owner who operates a public EV charging setup in Giridih, Jharkhand, explains the financial challenge faced by local businesses."In private dealer-owned fuel stations, the entire investment falls on the dealer," Sahu says. "Setting up a 60 kW DC charger costs around 8.5 to 9 lakh rupees for the machine alone. On top of that, buying a dedicated 63 kVA transformer takes another 5.5 to 6 lakh rupees in deposits and grid connection expenses. You end up spending 15 to 16 lakh rupees.""In small towns like Giridih, if only 2 to 4 vehicles show up a day, you can't recover your costs," Sahu adds. "That is why private pump dealers in Jharkhand and Bihar avoid installing them. The vehicles aren't there yet, and without footfall, nobody wants to lock in Rs 15 lakhs."This creates a cycle that is difficult to break. EV owners need chargers before they feel confident buying electric cars, but operators are reluctant to invest in chargers until there are enough EVs using them.To deal with low utilisation, operators are now looking at other business models.According to the Rubix report, charge point operators (CPOs) are moving towards fleet leasing contracts, revenue-sharing arrangements with site owners and open-roaming networks. These models can help operators get more regular usage and reduce the risk of investing in chargers that remain empty.Technical frameworks & heavy freight road aheadIndia is also trying to reduce fragmentation in its charging system. Standard-setting bodies such as the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) are working on charging standards and technologies that can make charging more uniform and suitable for different types of EVs.LECCS (light electric vehicle combined charging system): Under standards such as IS 17017 Part-2 Sec-7 and IS 17017 Part-31, LECCS combines AC charging of up to 7 kW and low-voltage DC charging of up to 12 kW into one standard plug for two and three-wheelers. The aim is to make charging more consistent instead of having different systems for different vehicles.Universal Sockets: These are intended for destination charging at places such as urban parking complexes. They can support charging from 2 kW to 22 kW using a standard Type-2 socket with detachable smart cables. This can reduce dependence on different proprietary charging systems.The bigger challenge will come with heavy commercial vehicles and long-distance transport. Chargers below 60 kW are generally not enough for trucks and other heavy vehicles that need to recharge quickly and get back on the road.DST frameworks therefore include much higher-powered charging systems. These include Split-Type DC chargers, which can dynamically distribute 40 kW to 240+ kW across several charging posts; Dual-Gun 500 kW systems; Overhead Pantographs offering up to 600 kW; and Megawatt Charging Systems (MCS), which can provide up to 3.75 MW of peak power for heavy logistics fleets.The difference in power is significant.A system designed for a scooter or a car used for city commuting cannot simply be used as the main charging solution for a fully loaded electric truck travelling long distances. As India's electric vehicle market moves towards larger commercial vehicles, the charging network will therefore need to become not only bigger, but much more powerful.Bridging the divideIndia’s transition to electric vehicles has moved beyond its early stage. As driver Siddharth Das prepares for his upcoming long-distance EV trip to Nepal, he is already planning his route around fast chargers, with charging stops mapped roughly every 150 km using route planners.Reaching the projected target of 13.2 lakhs by Rubix study by 2030 will require much more than simply adding chargers in existing EV hubs.The network will need to expand beyond major cities and states that already have a large share of the country's chargers. At the same time, operators will need easier transformer and grid connections, charging standards will need to become more consistent, and fast chargers will need to become more widely available on national highways.For consumers, the difference could determine whether an EV remains mainly a city vehicle or becomes a practical option for longer journeys across India.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Is UK heading for a breakup? Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland push for independence
articles.summary: UK News: Is the UK heading for a breakup? A fresh challenge is emerging as leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland prepare to join forces in a push f.
articles.body: Is the UK heading for a breakup? A fresh challenge is emerging as leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland prepare to join forces in a push for greater self-determination and the right to hold independence referendums.According to The Telegraph, the leaders of the three devolved nations are set to meet in Wales' Cardiff for an unprecedented summit, where they are expected to sign a joint declaration asserting their right to hold independence referendums and determine their own constitutional futures.The gathering comes at a politically sensitive moment for Westminster.UK PM Andy Burnham recently told MPs that he would authorise another Scottish independence referendum if there were a “clear consensus” in favour of one.The issue has gained further momentum after US President Donald Trump weighed in on Irish reunification. During a visit to Dublin on Saturday, Trump said he would “love” to see a united Ireland, describing Northern Ireland joining the Republic as “a great thing” and asking: “How can it be bad?”The comments have added to pressure on the Burnham-led UK government as nationalist parties push for a greater say over their nations’ futures. PM Burnham has made the devolution of power in England a central part of his political agenda.John Swinney, the SNP leader and Scottish first minister, has seized on the changing political landscape, claiming Burnham was “facing up to the idea that he will go down in history as the final prime minister of the United Kingdom”.Pro-independence parties gain groundThe balance of power across the devolved nations has shifted significantly following Labour’s poor performance in Wales at May’s elections. For the first time, pro-independence parties are now in government across Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.Plaid Cymru emerged as the largest party in the Cardiff Senedd, paving the way for its leader Rhun ap Iowerth to become Wales’ First Minister.In Scotland, the SNP remained the dominant political force despite losing six Holyrood seats, with Reform and the Greens making gains.Northern Ireland has also been under Sinn Fein leadership since Michelle O’Neill became First Minister in 2024. Sinn Fein had emerged as the largest party in the 2022 Stormont elections, although a DUP walkout delayed the formation of the executive. The party is widely expected to retain power when Northern Ireland votes again next year.The Cardiff summit will bring together the three first ministers along with Mary Lou McDonald, Sinn Fein’s president and leader of the opposition in Ireland.The leaders are expected to explore closer cooperation and discuss a renewed campaign for greater constitutional autonomy at the five-star St David’s Hotel overlooking Cardiff Bay.‘Status quo is not sustainable’Swinney said on Sunday: “For the first time ever, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are led by pro-independence first ministers. There could be no clearer sign that the status quo is not sustainable, and that Westminster must prepare for a post-UK future.“The momentum behind serious constitutional change is undeniable. Andy Burnham must now be facing up to the idea that he will go down in history as the final prime minister of the United Kingdom.“Tomorrow in Cardiff, I am looking forward to discussing a better future with partners from across these islands, and that only comes with the fresh start of independence.”The joint declaration is expected to underline the three nations’ claim to self-determination while putting further political pressure on Westminster.Burnham’s recent remarks have already opened the door to renewed debate over Scottish independence. During Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday, he said another referendum could be held if public opinion backed one.He told the House of Commons that the trigger for a separation vote was “exactly the same situation in Scotland” as Northern Ireland.The Good Friday Agreement provides a potential constitutional route for Northern Ireland to hold a referendum on reunification with Ireland. Under its terms, such a vote should be held if it “appears likely” that a majority of people in Northern Ireland would choose to leave the UK.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Cheyenne's Twin Chimneys motor court stood for almost 90 years; this week its landmark chimneys fell in about 30 seconds to make way for a drive-thru coffee shop
articles.summary: US News: The Twin Chimneys Motor Court in Cheyenne, Wyoming, which once gave travellers a place to stay along the historic Lincoln Highway, has been demolished.
articles.body: The Twin Chimneys Motor Court in Cheyenne, Wyoming, which once gave travellers a place to stay along the historic Lincoln Highway, has been demolished to make way for a 7 Brew Coffee drive-thru stand. Its distinctive twin stone chimneys, the last parts of the old motel to be removed, came down in about 30 seconds earlier this week.According to Cowboy State Daily, the motel at 2405 East Lincolnway had been known for its twin chimneys, red exterior, green roof and knotty pine interior. The motor court had provided lodging for travellers for decades, while also giving them a covered place to keep their cars next to their rooms.The demolition has drawn attention from many because the property was one of several old motor courts associated with travel along US Highway 30. Megan Stanfill, executive director of the Alliance for Historic Wyoming, said she was disappointed that the building was gone before there was a chance to consider ways of preserving it.“I always hate seeing old buildings torn down before there’s a chance to save them,” Stanfill told Cowboy State Daily. “Instead of preserving it as a motel, maybe the chimneys could have been preserved as a landmark.”Stanfill said discussions about giving old buildings a new use often happen only when it is already too late. She said she first noticed Twin Chimneys while driving past it and thought, “What a cool building.” A few months later, she saw that a fence had been put around the property.Why Twin Chimneys stood outStanfill began researching the history of the motel after noticing it. She said the rooms were original and dated to the time when the motor court was built in the 1930s, while the reception area was renovated during the mid-century era.Stanfill believes the twin chimneys may have been designed to help the motel stand out to passing travellers. In the 1930s, motor courts were competing for travellers' money and needed ways to make their properties easy to recognise.“Back in the 1930s, these places were competing for travelers' money, so they were trying to figure out the best way to appeal to them and make it easier for them to remember,” Stanfill said. “People didn’t have Google to figure out which motel to go to. They’d just hear about the Twin Chimneys a few states away.”The Lincoln Highway was a private transcontinental road whose construction began in 1913. Travellers using the road were not necessarily staying in traditional hotels. Instead, motor courts developed by offering both accommodation and a place to park a car.“They were camping out in their car,” Stanfill said. “People started offering lodging, a place for you to park your car where it was covered right next to your room.”Motor courts and the Lincoln HighwayStanfill said several examples of motor courts like Twin Chimneys still remain across Wyoming. They include the Sands Hotel in Cheyenne and other examples in Evanston and Fort Bridger.She has also stayed at renovated motor courts along the Lincoln Highway, including the Lincoln Highway Motor Court in Pennsylvania. According to Stanfill, its new owners are restoring the property and trying to create a place where travellers can experience the Lincoln Highway.She said there is growing interest in such properties across the country. She pointed to the popularity of Route 66, which is celebrating its centennial, as an example of interest in historic road travel.“It’s a bit of a revival, and people are looking for places like that,” she said. “I really hope we start seeing a lot more movement along those lines for the Lincoln Highway.”For Twin Chimneys, however, that opportunity has passed. The property owner had gone through the required city process for demolition, and Stanfill said there was no way for her organisation to stop it.‘Look at the pictures’While she was sad to see the entire property disappear, Stanfill said property owners ultimately have to decide what is best for their land.She added, “We can’t stop demolition like this; it’s already gone through the proper channels with the city. There’s nothing we can do at this point but look at the pictures we do have.”Stanfill said she would have liked to conduct a survey of the building and document it. Such records, she said, could have been useful when dealing with similar old buildings that are in poor condition.The demolition was carried out by Chuck Harter of McCarty & Sons, a Denver construction company. The twin chimneys were saved until the end of the demolition. Harter said the East Lincolnway lot would be cleared of all traces of Twin Chimneys in about three days.The new business planned for the site is a 7 Brew Coffee stand. The company already has a shop on Dell Range Boulevard in Cheyenne.Although the motel is gone, some reminders of Twin Chimneys remain in private collections. Stanfill said visitors used to take home matchbook covers and postcards from the property.“When people would visit they’d grab matchbook covers and postcards,” Stanfill said. “They had no idea there’d be something called eBay, with people selling this stuff for a pretty penny.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Altitude and attitude: How DGCA makes sure high-flying pilots don’t fly high
articles.summary: India News: There is something inherently unsettling about flying. Thirty thousand feet above the ground, hundreds of passengers sit inside a pressurised metal tu.
articles.body: There is something inherently unsettling about flying. Thirty thousand feet above the ground, hundreds of passengers sit inside a pressurised metal tube travelling at hundreds of kilometres per hour, trusting a handful of people with their lives for the duration of the journey. Yet every day, millions of us make this decision without thinking twice.And then, once in a blue moon, an incident happens that makes us pause and wonder just how much we can actually trust those handful of people.On August 4, an Air India A320 flying from Phuket to Delhi was cruising at 36,000 feet when it suddenly climbed 372 feet before dropping nearly 300 feet. Twenty-four people on board, including passengers and crew, were injured badly enough to require hospitalisation. Twenty were discharged shortly afterwards, while four sustained serious injuries and remained hospitalised for further treatment. Many passengers also took to social media and spoke to news reporters about how frightening the experience had been.A preliminary report shows that, over those eight seconds, the aircraft lost all three of its hydraulic systems and the autopilot disengaged. The hydraulic systems recovered within seconds, and the aircraft subsequently landed normally.On the surface, it was a technical failure. But a second finding in the incident became the headline across news outlets.As part of the standard procedure following such incidents, the crew is tested on various parameters to ensure that investigators have a complete picture of what happened. In this case, both pilots underwent the mandatory psychoactive-substance test after arriving in Delhi, a requirement for flights originating outside India.The co-pilot’s sample came back negative twice. The pilot-in-command’s report, however, raised concerns. The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau’s (AAIB) preliminary report used the term ‘non-negative’ to describe both the screening test and the confirmatory laboratory report.What was reported as ‘positive’ in headlines was not, in fact, the language used in the report. In aviation investigations, that distinction matters. The AAIB’s responsibility is not to point fingers, but to establish what happened and identify measures that can prevent a recurrence.The preliminary report does not conclude that substance use caused the hydraulic failure. It does, however, flag a serious concern regarding psychoactive substances and recommends that the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) take appropriate action.The DGCA is the apex regulatory body responsible for overseeing safety standards in civil aviation. Its rulebook is extensive and is regularly revised to address emerging risks and ensure that flying remains safe for passengers and crew.Alcohol testing has been mandatory since the mid-2000s. The framework was built around Rule 24 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, which originally required that crew members not consume alcohol within 12 hours of a flight. The rule has since been revised several times. A 2023 revision, for instance, warned that medicines and other substances containing alcohol could trigger a breathalyser reading, specifically citing products such as mouthwash and tooth gel. Crew members taking medication are required to consult their company doctor before flying.For scheduled operators, flight and cabin crew are subject to pre-flight breathalyser testing at the first departure airport during a duty period. For flights originating outside India, post-flight testing is required at the first Indian airport of landing.Being fit to fly is a regulatory requirement. But while the rules around alcohol have been in place for decades, psychoactive substances present a more complicated challenge.Drug testing is relatively new. The DGCA introduced the framework based on a 2019 report by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, which estimated that 2.8% of Indians had used cannabis in the previous year and 2.1% had used opioids. From 2019 to 2026, these numbers have only increased.These figures should not be taken as evidence that aviation personnel use drugs. Rather, they indicate the potential scale of the threat that the misuse of psychoactive substances can pose to aviation safety.What happens when a pilot gets tested for drugs?The drug-testing system applies to flight crew and air traffic controllers. Testing is required before employment, following accidents, through random checks and as follow-up in previously confirmed cases.Random testing is currently designed to cover at least 10% of an organisation’s employees each year at specified airports. The testing panel is broad, covering substances including amphetamines, methamphetamines, cocaine, opioids, benzodiazepines, marijuana/hashish, MDMA and several others.The system is also designed around confirmation, rather than treating an initial screening result as conclusive. It is consequently more time- and resource-intensive than an alcohol test.A urine sample is divided into A and B portions. The initial screening is conducted under controlled conditions. If the A sample screens positive, the B sample is sent to a DGCA-authorised laboratory for confirmatory testing, with procedures in place to maintain the chain of custody.A person who returns a positive screening result is removed from safety-sensitive duties until the confirmatory report is received.If a first confirmed positive is established, the rules provide for de-addiction and rehabilitation, followed by repeat testing and clearance from a treating psychiatrist and the organisation’s chief medical officer before the person can return to active duty.A second confirmed positive, however, carries a far more severe consequence: cancellation of the licence.In other words, the regulatory system is built around two competing principles: aviation cannot afford to ignore substance use, but neither can it treat every initial test result as proof of impairment or permanently write off a person without due process.Crew perspectiveTOI spoke to aviation personnel to understand their perspective on the DGCA rules governing substance use in the industry.A senior pilot lauded the system, saying the DGCA maintains strict standards to protect the safety of the countless passengers who entrust their lives to the aviation system every day. But he said the responsibility does not rest with the regulator alone. A moral responsibility also falls on the crew entrusted with those lives.“The number of variables when it comes to substances in the market has increased and having access to them has become easier, but that does not mean that it can be used as an excuse. A soldier at the border is stressed too, but he has a responsibility to his nation to do his duty properly and honestly. So do we,” the pilot, who did not wish to be named, said.A cabin crew member, meanwhile, said drinking after work and, in some cases, using substances is not unheard of among crew. But she said there is a clear boundary between what happens off duty and the responsibilities that come with being in the air, and that most crew understand the implications of bringing such behaviour into the workplace.At the same time, she pointed to the pressures that come with the job.“I have been grounded for acne, for weight gain, I was once even grounded because my nails were too long,” she said.For cabin crew, the demands of the job extend beyond safety procedures and passenger service. Strict appearance standards, long and irregular working hours and constant interaction with passengers can add to the pressures of a profession in which employees are expected to maintain a high standard of presentation and hospitality at all times.These pressures, however, are difficult to separate from the broader conversation around substance use.It is this tension that sits at the heart of the debate. The pressures of the job are real, and an environment that leaves people constantly stressed can create conditions in which some may turn to alcohol or other substances. But for those sitting in the cockpit, stress cannot become an explanation for abandoning the responsibility that comes with the job.The net gets widerThe Phuket incident has already prompted the regulator to widen that net.The DGCA has directed Indian airlines to conduct a one-time psychoactive-substance test on all their pilots by July 2027. The exercise will cover the country’s nearly 14,000 airline pilots. Air India had already begun its own one-time testing programme for about 5,000 pilots across Air India and Air India Express following the August 4 incident.The move comes as the DGCA works on a revision of its existing rules governing psychoactive-substance testing. The current framework requires random testing, with organisations expected to cover at least 10% of their employees annually. The proposed changes are expected to make the system more stringent.The senior pilot said the next step could also involve newer testing methods capable of delivering conclusive results faster, allowing airlines to test a much larger pool of crew rather than relying primarily on periodic random checks.The DGCA can test, regulate and punish. Airlines can monitor and intervene. But ultimately, the last line of defence is also the person sitting in the cockpit.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Poland alarmed after Russia attacks train from Kiev to Warsaw
articles.summary: After Russian attacks on a train from Kiev to Warsaw and on Ukraine's border region with Poland, the Polish government on Sunday accused Moscow of escalating...
articles.body:
Polish government accuses Moscow of escalating conflict after Russian attacks on train from Kiev to Warsaw and Ukraine's border region with Poland.

Ukrainian President Zelensky calls for tougher consequences on Moscow after attacks near Polish-Ukrainian border set a locomotive on fire and damaged a petrol station.

Moscow confirms attacks on rail infrastructure in western Ukraine facilitating transport of military goods from European countries, as Ukraine continues to defend itself against Russian invasion.

After Russian attacks on a train from Kiev to Warsaw and on Ukraine's border region with Poland, the Polish government on Sunday accused Moscow of escalating the conflict.

"Putin escalates," Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski wrote on X. Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened a crisis team for the afternoon. Western politicians travelling to Kiev rely on the rail link from Poland to Ukraine as the country's airspace is closed.

On Sunday, the locomotive of the passenger train from Kiev to Warsaw was attacked at the border station of Yahodyn, according to Ukrainian Railways. Passengers were evacuated in time and nobody was harmed, it said.

Polish railway operator PKP said it had taken over the train from the Ukrainian side with a delay of more than six hours and it was continuing on to Warsaw.

Poland's Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said a drone also struck in western Ukraine one kilometre from Poland's border and another at a distance of five kilometres. Polish F-16 fighter jets and a reconnaissance aircraft monitored the situation, he said. Polish airspace was not violated.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote that Moscow's attacks near the Polish-Ukrainian border in the Volyn region set a locomotive on fire and damaged a petrol station.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called for tougher consequences on Moscow. Russian attacks on the Polish-Ukrainian border were not simply a continuation of attacks on Ukraine's state borders, he wrote on X.

"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he said.

Prime Minister Tusk convened a late-afternoon crisis meeting of cabinet ministers and uniformed services. "We are taking these events extremely seriously," Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote on X.

The Defence Ministry in Moscow confirmed attacks on rail infrastructure in western Ukraine that facilitated transport of military goods from European countries, it said.

Ukraine has been defending itself with Western help for more than four and a half years against a Russian invasion. Russian attacks repeatedly cause deaths and damage to rail traffic and at stations.

articles.title: Brics diplomacy: Iran president says Tehran, UAE want to 'turn the page' on war
articles.summary: Middle East News: NEW DELHI: A day after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met UAE Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A day after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met UAE Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the Brics Summit in New Delhi, Tehran signalled a push to move past the conflict and strengthen ties with its Gulf neighbour.Pezeshkian said Iran had no problems with the UAE or other regional countries, drawing a distinction between Tehran's relations with its neighbours and its opposition to US military bases in the region. His remarks came after the meeting with the UAE leadership at a time when the West Asia conflict has strained relations across the region.“We have no problems with the UAE. We have no problem with any of the regional countries. We have a problem with the American bases located in these countries and from which they are attacking our country,” Pezeshkian said.Pezeshkian said Iran considered the UAE and other Gulf states to be “brothers” and expressed a desire to expand relations with them. “The UAE, the Emiratis and other countries of the region are our brothers. We have been living together for a long time and we have had trade. We have supported each other,” he said.Also read: Brics hammers out joint declaration after India bridges Iran-UAE chasmIran draws line between UAE and US basesPezeshkian on Saturday said Tehran's objection was directed at the use of territory in neighbouring countries by the United States rather than at the Gulf states themselves.“So this is the US that has come here and established bases, and from those bases they martyr our children, they attack our infrastructure and bomb, and they target our leaders, commanders and people,” he said.“In fact, the problem is that the friendly and neighbouring countries should not allow enemies to utilise their soil to attack our country,” the Iranian President added.He said Tehran wanted to strengthen ties with the UAE and other neighbouring countries. “Right now, we have a good relation with the UAE and we can expand it, and with other countries, the same happened. So we would like to have a sincere relation with all of them,” Pezeshkian said.The Iranian President also accused the United States of seeking to exploit the region's energy resources while using arms sales to deepen divisions among regional countries.“However, it is the US which does not want this to happen,” he said, alleging that Washington wanted to "utilise our petroleum reservoirs of the region” while selling weapons and missiles to regional countries “in order to scare us from each other and pit us against each other.”“It is actually exploiting the capital of the region and also it is destroying the peace and stability,” Pezeshkian said.Iran, UAE leaders meet in DelhiPezeshkian's comments came a day after his meeting with UAE Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the Brics Summit in New Delhi.The meeting brought the Iranian and Emirati leadership together as the expanded Brics grouping discussed the escalating conflict in West Asia. Details of the talks were not immediately made public.The meeting was significant against the backdrop of tensions between Iran and several Gulf states over the wider regional conflict. The UAE has also maintained security partnerships with Western powers, a point repeatedly criticised by Tehran.The New Delhi Summit nevertheless provided a platform for direct engagement between regional powers that have differed over the conflict.Pezeshkian calls for regional cooperationPezeshkian said Iran wanted neighbouring countries to pool their capabilities to improve regional security and promote economic and cultural ties.“We, with the neighbouring and regional countries, can share our powers in order to help each other and establish security and help our people in order to promote our culture and economy again,” he said.His remarks came as the Brics Summit sought to build consensus on the escalating West Asia crisis, with the conflict emerging as a major issue during discussions in New Delhi.Also read: UN hails Iran-UAE meeting on sidelines of Brics Summit, says India can be 'bridge-builder'Brics declaration calls for restraintBrics leaders adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026, expressing serious concern over the escalation in West Asia and calling for maximum restraint, dialogue and diplomacy.The declaration called for the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure and stressed the importance of maintaining global trade, supply chains and energy flows amid the conflict.It also expressed concern over attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards, stressing that nuclear safety and security must be maintained even during armed conflicts.The declaration called for the implementation of relevant UN General Assembly and Security Council resolutions and urged all parties to maintain a ceasefire and ensure full and unhindered humanitarian access to the Gaza Strip.The Iran-UAE engagement in New Delhi, followed by Pezeshkian's comments on closer regional ties, came as the Brics platform sought to position itself as a forum for dialogue and diplomacy amid the continuing West Asia crisis.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Su-57 for India: Can Russia’s stealth fighter counter Pakistan’s China-backed J-35 plan?
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Su-57 has emerged as one of the key defence proposals in focus during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India for the Brics s.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Su-57 has emerged as one of the key defence proposals in focus during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India for the Brics summit, reopening a long-running question for New Delhi: should it acquire an off-the-shelf fifth-generation fighter from Russia while developing its own Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), or wait for the indigenous programme to mature?Russia has repeatedly offered India the Su-57, its fifth-generation multirole fighter, including a proposal for joint production and deeper technology cooperation. Ahead of the Brics summit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the issue of supplying Su-57 fighters remained on the agenda between Moscow and New Delhi.The Kremlin’s position was stated on September 8, when Peskov said: "ISSUES OF SELLING SU-57 IS ON THE AGENDA BETWEEN INDIA AND RUSSIA"The issue assumed greater significance as Putin arrived in New Delhi for the Brics summit and held talks with PM Modi. Defence cooperation was among the areas expected to figure in the discussions, alongside energy, trade, technology and other strategic issues. Russian proposals reportedly include Su-57 cooperation as well as upgrades for India’s existing Su-30MKI fleet.There is, however, no publicly confirmed Indian decision to induct the Su-57. The question therefore remains whether Russia's offer can provide India with an interim fifth-generation capability without undermining the country's longer-term AMCA ambitions.Why India needs a fifth-generation fighterIndia currently does not operate an indigenous or foreign fifth-generation fighter, while China has built a rapidly expanding fleet of J-20 stealth fighters and is moving ahead with the J-35 programme. Pakistan is also pursuing closer military aviation cooperation with China, including reported plans for the J-35.This creates a significant capability gap for the Indian Air Force.The IAF has also been dealing with a shortage of fighter squadrons. Its authorised strength is 42 squadrons, while the actual number has remained substantially lower. The situation is complicated by an ageing fleet, delays in new aircraft deliveries and the long development timeline associated with a fifth-generation indigenous aircraft.The AMCA is intended to fill that gap in the long term. The government has moved the programme into a more concrete development phase, with the defence ministry issuing a request for proposal in May 2026 to three Indian private-sector-led bidders for the design and development of prototypes.But AMCA will still take years to become an operational combat aircraft. That creates the central dilemma for India: how to address the fifth-generation capability gap during the period before AMCA enters service.What Russia is offering IndiaRussia's proposition is attractive on paper because it combines an operational fifth-generation platform with the possibility of industrial cooperation.Putin had offered India joint production of the Su-57 and said Moscow was prepared to cooperate without "limitations". The proposal has been presented as an opportunity to manufacture the fighter in India and potentially deepen technology cooperation under the Make in India framework.However, some of the more ambitious claims surrounding the proposal, including the precise extent of access to software source code, technology and intellectual property, should not be treated as final terms unless they are incorporated into a formal agreement.The same applies to reports that India could initially receive a specific number of aircraft before local production begins. No final publicly announced contract establishing such a production and delivery schedule has been confirmed.For India, the attraction is therefore not simply the aircraft itself. It is the possibility of obtaining a fifth-generation platform while simultaneously building domestic manufacturing and maintenance capabilities around it.Su-57 vs Rafale: Different answers to different problemsThe Su-57 and Rafale should not be viewed as direct substitutes. Rafale is a mature 4.5-generation multirole fighter with an established operational record and a large international user base. The Su-57 is designed as a low-observable fifth-generation fighter with internal weapons carriage, advanced sensors, high manoeuvrability and a substantially different combat philosophy.India's reported plan to acquire 114 additional Rafales is aimed primarily at increasing overall fighter strength and replacing older aircraft. The Rafale therefore addresses India's immediate force-structure problem.The Su-57 would address a different requirement: giving the IAF access to a fifth-generation capability before AMCA becomes operational.The distinction is important because buying more Rafales does not eliminate India's stealth-fighter gap. Conversely, buying Su-57s would not by itself solve the IAF's broader shortage of fighter squadrons.India could therefore theoretically pursue both tracks: Rafale for near-term squadron strength and Su-57 or AMCA for the fifth-generation requirement. The difficulty would be cost, manpower, infrastructure, logistics, training and the need to maintain multiple fighter ecosystems.Why the Su-57 remains attractiveThe strongest argument for the Su-57 is timing. AMCA is India's strategically important long-term answer, but the aircraft is still in development. A mature indigenous fifth-generation fighter cannot simply be accelerated into operational service without accepting substantial technological and developmental risks.The Su-57 already exists as a flying and operational Russian platform. Russia says the aircraft has been used in combat operations, although the extent and nature of its combat employment are not independently transparent enough to establish broad claims of battlefield superiority.The aircraft also offers characteristics that India could value in its geographical environment. It combines low-observable design with high speed, long range, internal weapons carriage and high manoeuvrability. It is designed as a multirole aircraft rather than solely as a stealth interceptor.The Russian fighter's large airframe and emphasis on range and weapons carriage could also be relevant to India's requirement for long-range operations across both the western and northern theatres.But these advantages should not be exaggerated. Radar cross-section, detailed sensor performance, electronic-warfare effectiveness and many other critical parameters remain classified or unavailable for reliable independent comparison.Su-57 vs F-35: Stealth is not the whole storyThe American F-35 is the most widely deployed and exported fifth-generation fighter programme in the world. It has a much larger production base, extensive international participation and a mature ecosystem of training, maintenance, software and allied operations.The Su-57 takes a different approach. The Russian aircraft places greater emphasis on a combination of low observability, speed, manoeuvrability, range and weapons. The F-35 places exceptional emphasis on stealth, sensor fusion, electronic warfare, situational awareness and network-centric operations.That makes the question of which aircraft is "better" difficult to answer in isolation.The F-35 has a major advantage in operational maturity, fleet size, international deployment and networking. The Su-57 can claim advantages in areas such as speed, manoeuvrability and potentially range, although exact comparative figures are difficult to independently verify.Russian industry officials have made much stronger claims. United Aircraft Corporation CEO Vadim Badekha said: "The Su-57 is the only fifth-generation aircraft in the world that is actually seeing combat and demonstrating its superiority over the best foreign weapons systems every single day. Our friends are well aware of this. We can say with confidence that the F-35 is not being considered on the Indian market today,"The statement should be understood as a Russian industry assessment rather than an independently established ranking of fifth-generation fighters.Su-57 vs China's J-20 and J-35China presents India with a more immediate strategic challenge than any Western fighter programme.The People's Liberation Army Air Force has already fielded the J-20 in significant numbers, while China is advancing the J-35, a second stealth-fighter programme aimed at expanding its fifth-generation capabilities.The J-20 and Su-57 also reflect different design priorities. The J-20 is generally associated with long-range air combat, low observability and the ability to engage targets beyond visual range. Its large airframe allows substantial internal weapons carriage and long-range operations.The Su-57 puts greater emphasis on multirole capability, manoeuvrability and a combination of stealth with conventional fighter performance. China's advantage, however, extends beyond the aircraft itself. Beijing has a much larger industrial base for producing combat aircraft and is building an increasingly sophisticated network of airborne early-warning aircraft, electronic warfare systems, long-range missiles, drones and other supporting assets.That ecosystem matters because modern air warfare is increasingly determined by sensors, data links, electronic warfare and long-range missiles rather than by the performance of a fighter in a one-on-one dogfight.The J-20 should therefore not be dismissed simply because the Su-57 may have advantages in speed or manoeuvrability.Where US, Russia and China standThe United States remains the most mature fifth-generation fighter power, with the F-35 programme operating across a large international network. The F-22 Raptor also remains an important American air-superiority platform, although it is not available for export.China has the J-20 and is expanding its fifth-generation capabilities through the J-35. Russia has the Su-57, but its fleet is considerably smaller than the American F-35 fleet or China's J-20 force.The comparison therefore goes beyond aircraft specifications. The US has the advantage of scale, combat experience, global basing and an extensive network of partner air forces. China has the advantage of industrial scale, rapid production and a rapidly expanding military aerospace ecosystem. Russia has a smaller fifth-generation fleet but offers India something Washington and Beijing are unlikely to offer on the same terms: extensive defence-industrial cooperation built around decades of military ties.Why Russia remains India's most practical partnerFor India, Russia's biggest advantage may not be that the Su-57 is universally superior to the F-35 or J-20. It is that Moscow has historically been more willing to pursue deep industrial cooperation with New Delhi.India and Russia have decades of experience in licensed production and joint defence projects, including the Su-30MKI and BrahMos programme.That existing ecosystem matters when considering a fighter expected to remain in service for several decades.Russia's willingness to discuss local production, technology cooperation and modifications could also provide India greater freedom to adapt the aircraft to its own weapons and operational requirements, subject to the final contractual terms.There is another consideration: India already operates a large Russian-origin combat fleet. The Su-30MKI forms a major part of the IAF's fighter inventory. A Russian fifth-generation aircraft could therefore potentially offer some commonality in training, weapons, maintenance philosophy and logistics, although the Su-57 would still represent a major new technological ecosystem. This is where the Russian proposal becomes strategically relevant.But the Su-57 could also create problemsThe biggest risk is that India could end up investing heavily in another foreign fighter programme just as it is attempting to establish AMCA as the centrepiece of its indigenous aerospace industry.India's earlier experience with the Fifth Generation Fighter Aircraft programme with Russia is a major cautionary example.India and Russia had agreed in 2007 to jointly develop a fifth-generation fighter based on the Russian programme. The project eventually stalled amid disagreements over cost, design, technology access and other issues, and India subsequently focused on developing its own fifth-generation aircraft.The current Su-57 proposal is therefore not simply a new aircraft purchase. It raises the question of whether India wants to repeat a major foreign fighter-development partnership while AMCA is already moving ahead.A large Su-57 programme could consume money, engineering resources and industrial capacity that India needs for AMCA.There is also the geopolitical dimension. India has expanded defence cooperation with the United States, France and other Western countries while maintaining its long-standing relationship with Moscow. A major new Russian fighter programme could complicate this balancing act, particularly because India's future fighter ecosystem will depend on Western technology in areas where domestic capability remains limited.Why Su-57 could still make sense as an interim solutionThe strongest case for the Su-57 is therefore not that India should abandon AMCA. It is that India could use a limited number of Su-57s as a bridge until AMCA becomes operational.Such an approach would give the IAF experience operating a fifth-generation platform, allow Indian personnel to develop expertise in low-observable aircraft, sensors, electronic warfare and internal weapons carriage, and potentially provide an operational capability against China's expanding stealth-fighter fleet.A limited acquisition would also reduce the risk of committing the bulk of India's fighter-modernisation budget to another long-term foreign programme.However, even a limited fleet would require dedicated infrastructure, training, maintenance, spares and weapons. A fighter's acquisition cost is only one part of its lifetime expense.The real choice: Buy time or build the futureIndia's fighter dilemma is ultimately about time. Rafale can help address the immediate fighter shortage. AMCA is designed to provide the long-term indigenous fifth-generation capability. The Su-57 sits between the two, offering a potentially faster route to a fifth-generation aircraft while creating an opportunity for deeper cooperation with Russia.That makes the Russian proposal difficult to ignore. But India does not need to choose the Su-57 because Russia says it is superior to every rival. Nor should it reject the aircraft simply because AMCA is India's preferred long-term option.The decision should rest on what Moscow is actually prepared to put into a binding agreement: the price, production rights, technology access, weapons integration, software access, maintenance support, delivery schedule, localisation, future upgrades and guarantees against supply disruption.If those conditions are favourable, the Su-57 could provide India with a bridge to the AMCA era. If they are not, diverting resources from AMCA to another foreign fighter programme could repeat the very dependency India is trying to overcome.For New Delhi, the most compelling argument for the Su-57 is therefore not that it is definitively the world's best fifth-generation fighter. It is that Russia may be willing to offer India a combination of a fifth-generation aircraft, local production and deeper industrial cooperation at a time when the IAF has a capability gap that AMCA cannot immediately fill.The final question for India is whether that bridge is worth the cost, and whether it can be built without delaying the indigenous fighter that is ultimately supposed to replace the need for such a bridge.

articles.title: Trump rejects calls to slow AI, says US leads China in technology
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump on Sunday said the United States is leading China in artificial intelligence and must maintain its edge, declaring that “who.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Sunday said the United States is leading China in artificial intelligence and must maintain its edge, declaring that “whoever wins AI wins” as he pushed back against calls for the industry to slow down or face tighter regulation.“We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told reporters when asked if the AI industry should slow down or be more regulated.Trump acknowledged that authorities could introduce safeguards for AI but said concerns being raised about the technology were often exaggerated.“We could put guardrails. We can do this and that. But I think you have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen,” Trump said.His comments come as the United States and China compete for dominance in AI, with Washington seeking to preserve its technological advantage in a rapidly evolving industry.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump blames Zelenskyy for diesel shortage, tells Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian supplies
articles.summary: US News: US president Donald Trump on Sunday urged Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel supplies, arguing that the attacks .
articles.body: US president Donald Trump on Sunday urged Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel supplies, arguing that the attacks were contributing to a fuel shortage.Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf club, Trump was asked whether he had spoken to Zelenskyy following his recent conversation with Russian president Vladimir Putin.“Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said, adding that Ukrainian forces have “plenty of other targets” they could strike. Destroying Russian diesel production capacity was “hurting the world”, he said, according to Bloomberg.Diesel prices in the US hit a record average of over $6 a gallon on Friday, as Ukraine’s strikes on Russia’s energy sector and disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz tightened global supplies, adding pressure on American consumers ahead of November’s midterm elections. Meanwhile, Ukraine has stepped up long-range strikes on Russian energy infrastructure in recent months, with Kyiv arguing that the oil and gas sector helps finance Russia’s war. The attacks have contributed to fuel rationing in parts of Russia.The latest strikes came as both countries exchanged large-scale drone attacks overnight.In Russia’s Tatarstan, two people were killed and 14 injured following a drone attack near Nizhnekamsk, according to regional authorities. The city hosts major oil-refining and petrochemical facilities.The office of regional head Rustam Minnikhanov said the two victims died when a drone struck a tree near their parked car. Nizhnekamsk mayor Radmir Belyaev separately reported a fire at an unspecified “enterprise”.Ukraine’s defence intelligence agency said it had also struck the Slavyansk-on-Kuban oil refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar region, claiming its drones hit an oil-processing unit and the facility’s tank farm.Krasnodar authorities said three people were injured, an oil pipeline was damaged and a fire broke out at an “enterprise”, without directly confirming Ukraine’s account.Russia’s defence ministry said 389 Ukrainian drones had been intercepted overnight.Ukraine also reported fresh Russian attacks. Serhii Lysak, head of Odesa’s military administration, said at least nine people were injured in what he described as a “massive” overnight assault on the Black Sea port city.Ukrainian authorities also reported a drone strike near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk crossing with Poland, where a petrol station caught fire. Ukraine’s air force said its defences had shot down or suppressed 409 Russian drones out of 453 launched overnight.Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was open to resuming trilateral peace talks with Ukraine and the US in October.“We are not ruling out that possibility. We are specifically talking about the foreseeable future. That is, October cannot be ruled out,” Peskov told reporters.The comments come after recent meetings involving US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, Putin and Zelenskyy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Australia switched on a $7.8 million wastewater plant that can process 700 megalitres a year; its inventor says it breaks down stubborn pollutants 16 times more efficiently
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Australia has switched on a new advanced wastewater treatment plant in regional New South Wales that could turn discarded sewage effluent into a valua.
articles.body: Australia has switched on a new advanced wastewater treatment plant in regional New South Wales that could turn discarded sewage effluent into a valuable source of recycled water. The $7.8 million facility in Dubbo can process up to 700 megalitres of wastewater a year, roughly the equivalent of 280 Olympic-sized swimming pools, as the region looks to strengthen its water security. ABC News reported the facility was switched on this week, while Squadron Energy, which helped fund the project, confirmed its capacity and cost.A new approach to treating difficult pollutantsAt the centre of the project is a wastewater treatment technology developed by water treatment scientist Troy Warry. According to Warry, the system can break down stubborn pollutants around 16 times more efficiently than conventional advanced oxidation systems.The technology uses a titanium-dioxide-based catalyst that remains permanently fixed inside the reactor while continuing to be activated by light. Unlike processes that simply filter contaminants out of wastewater, the system is designed to chemically break down pollutants.That includes difficult-to-remove substances such as pesticides, petroleum hydrocarbons, pharmaceutical residues, antibiotics, hormones and other persistent organic compounds, according to the technology’s developer. ABC reported that the system was previously trialled in Germany, Spain and Norway.Warry’s claimed efficiency advantage is significant, but it remains his assessment of the technology rather than an independently established performance benchmark. University of Sydney civil engineering professor Stuart Khan told ABC that the approach was relatively uncommon at this scale and that results would need to be assessed before its broader impact could be determined.Why Dubbo is betting on recycled wastewaterThe plant has been built beside Dubbo’s existing Sewerage Treatment Plant through a public-private partnership between Dubbo Regional Council and renewable energy company Squadron Energy.Squadron Energy contributed $3.6 million towards the project, with the arrangement initially allowing the company to access recycled water for construction associated with its renewable energy developments in the region. The company’s investment was framed as part of a wider effort to reduce pressure on local water supplies.The facility’s 700-megalitre annual capacity represents about 11% of Dubbo’s annual water use, according to Squadron Energy. The company and council have said the infrastructure is intended to provide a longer-term water-security benefit beyond the construction of renewable energy projects.From wastewater to a new water resourceThe recycled water is not yet approved for every proposed use. Dubbo Regional Council is working through approvals for applications including dust suppression and concrete batching, while further testing is being undertaken with the University of Newcastle to assess other potential uses, including irrigation of sporting facilities.The technology could be particularly relevant to inland communities because it offers an alternative to membrane-based treatment such as reverse osmosis. Professor Khan noted that such filtration processes can leave behind concentrated salty waste, creating another disposal challenge in inland areas.For Dubbo, the bigger idea is not simply treating sewage more efficiently. It is changing the role of wastewater itself, from something to be discarded into a resource that can supplement supplies when drought, population growth and increasingly unpredictable rainfall put pressure on conventional water sources.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
